Being emotionally close or intimate with others

issues.item: Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma, 'comments on family' is not impossible as a trigger, but paired with the rest of the profile it lacks a clear assault-linked context. The other triggers and memory items point to sensory/intrusive re-experiencing, whereas this item suggests a family-related theme not represented elsewhere in threat, appraisals, or memory.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid grief reminders' implies a bereavement/loss-focused coping target, but no other selected items indicate death loss or grief as a central aspect of the assault trauma. This maladaptive strategy does not fit the rest of the profile, which centers on assault-related intrusive memory, dissociation, and social avoidance.

vignette: Thomas, a 68-year-old school counselor in a small Midwestern town, had spent the better part of his life helping adolescents navigate the chaos of adolescence. He was married to his college sweetheart, Maria, and they had two grown children who now lived in other states. His calm, steady demeanor in the school's health office belied a quiet, gnawing fear that had lingered since a violent assault he endured in his thirties. On a humid summer night in 1985, a disgruntled neighbor burst into his apartment, knife in hand. Thomas tried to defend himself, but the attacker struck him repeatedly in the chest, left a jagged wound on his sternum, and hauled him to the emergency department. The antiseptic sting of the hospital, the buzzing of fluorescent lights, and the metallic taste of blood became indelibly linked in Thomas's mind to that night of terror. The very scent of antiseptic that Thomas once tolerated while checking students' health records now sends a rush of panic through him. When he steps into the school's health office, the faint odor of cleaning solutions-so familiar to his students-evokes a snapshot memory of the hospital corridor, the sight of his own bleeding, the hiss of the air-conditioning system, and the pounding of his heart. Each recollection is a clear picture that flashes before his eyes, and the terror he felt at the time resurges with equal intensity. The smell of alcohol, too, has become a trigger; whenever he passes the faculty lounge where colleagues discuss their day over wine, the scent of fermented grape overwhelms him, dredging up a fragment of the night he once tried to drown his pain in a cramped bar. When a partner or student reaches out for emotional closeness, Thomas feels a sudden surge of dread-he remembers the warmth that once felt like a threat, the way a hug could feel like a hand reaching out to hold him again. Because of these vivid, terrifying memories, Thomas has learned to protect himself by deliberately dissociating whenever a trigger surfaces. He feels as if he is stepping outside his own body, a numbing escape that allows him to survive the onslaught of pain. The terror on recall pushes him to avoid people entirely; he resists student inquiries, shuns colleagues' friendly chatter, and declines invitations to social events, fearing that proximity might bring him back to that night of vulnerability. Avoiding intimacy has become a second layer of defense; he keeps his wife emotionally distant, insisting that any attempt at closeness is a potential threat that could lead to his body becoming a target once more. These maladaptive strategies in turn reinforce the presence of triggers in Thomas's life. By avoiding people, he spends most of his days alone in the health office, where the antiseptic scent of cleaning supplies is most potent. The isolation forces him to confront the very smell he seeks to escape, tightening the loop of fear. His avoidance of intimacy with Maria means that their evenings are quiet and devoid of conversation, a quiet that amplifies the memory of the hospital's sterile silence. When he declines invitations to faculty gatherings, he finds himself alone in the cramped faculty lounge, listening to others' laughter and the clink of glasses, which brings the alcohol smell-and the associated traumatic memory-into sharper focus. The more Thomas isolates himself, the more he encounters the very triggers that drove him to isolate, and the more he feels compelled to retreat again. The mounting isolation has begun to erode the marriage that had once been his anchor. Maria has noticed that Thomas has become increasingly withdrawn and has begged him to seek professional help. The fear that his avoidance may lead to the loss of their partnership has pushed him to schedule an intake appointment. He hopes that, by confronting the triggers and the memories they ignite, he can break the self-reinforcing cycle of avoidance and dissociation. What keeps him hopeful is the conviction that he is not doomed to live forever in the shadow of that night; what terrifies him most is the possibility that, if he continues on his current path, the memories and triggers will continue to dictate his days, driving him further into isolation and away from the life he has built.
